name: Pottery in Neolithic Upper Mesopotamia and the northern Levant
summary: Farming villages of northern Syria and neighbouring regions began making fired clay vessels around 7000 to 6900 BCE, the start of pottery in Southwest Asia.
description: Radiocarbon dates put the beginning of pottery production in southeastern Anatolia, the upper Euphrates, Upper Mesopotamia and the northern Levant at about 7000 to 6900 BCE, the last major innovation of the Neolithic there, long after farming. At Tell Sabi Abyad and Shir the first vessels were few, small, mineral-tempered and often decorated, not crude experiments. Where within the region the craft was first worked out is not known.

impact.note: Pottery became universal across Southwest Asia and the societies that drew on it (many societies, but importance.md reserves reach 3 for the East Asian origin); fired containers were a new capability for cooking and storage; and a long line of ceramic work followed in the region, though the specific descendants named by the lead are not sourced.

date.label: around 7000 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Nieuwenhuyse concluded that the ceramics in the earliest pottery layers at Tell Sabi Abyad and Shir, dating to around 7000 BCE, were not necessarily the result of earlier local experiments.

evidence.supports: dating to around 7000 BCE, were not necessarily the result of experiments that took place at older, yet-to-be discovered
evidence.locator: Chapter 2, Spoor, A Man Feasting. Olivier's Journey through Archaeology

date.label: around 7000/6900 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Ten radiocarbon dates from the lowest layers at Shir, which hold its earliest pottery, appear to confirm a date around 7000 to 6900 BCE.

evidence.supports: By contrast, at Shir ten 14C dates from the lowest layers 0 and I appear to confirm a date around 7000/ 6900 BCE
evidence.locator: Chapter 10, Bartl, Pottery Development in the 7th millennium BCE in the Northern, Central, and Southern Levant, p. 163

date.label: around 7000/6900 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Across southeastern Anatolia, the upper Euphrates and Upper Mesopotamia the period around 7000 to 6900 BCE can be regarded as the beginning of pottery production, with no single centre of origin identified.

evidence.supports: the period around 7000/6900 BCE can be regarded as the beginning of pottery production in all these regions, so that the question of the spread of production knowledge from a specific centre of origin appears irrelevant

date.label: c. 7000-6700 BCE
date.basis: As the cited source gives it.

events.statement: Very early ceramics of the Initial Pottery Neolithic at Tell Sabi Abyad come from levels comparable to the lowest levels of the main mound, dated to about 7000 to 6700 BCE.

evidence.supports: The investigation yielded very early ceramics ascribed to the so-called Initial Pottery Neolithic. The levels are comparable to those found in the lowest levels at the main mound of Tell Sabi Abyad I, ca. 7000-6700 BCE.
evidence.locator: Chapter 5, Connan et al., Chemical Study of Bitumens from Tell Sabi Abyad

earliest_record.rationale: The earliest dated evidence found for this capability in this community. No review has yet confirmed that nothing earlier exists.

unresolved.note: Read Nieuwenhuyse, Akkermans and van der Plicht, Not so coarse, nor always plain: the earliest pottery of Syria (Antiquity 84, 2010), and Tsuneki, Nieuwenhuyse and Campbell (eds), The Emergence of Pottery in West Asia (2017), for the primary dates and for where the craft was first worked out.
The coordinates of Tell Sabi Abyad and Shir are from the supervisor's memory, not from the source; check them against a gazetteer.
Bartl leaves open whether pottery at Tell Halula is older than 7000 BCE.

research.note: The volume says pottery began at about the same time across the region, so that a single centre of origin 'appears irrelevant', and that the first pots at Sabi Abyad and Shir were adopted from unnamed communities; nothing read shows either independence from, or a link to, the older pottery of Africa and East Asia.
